questions.prompt: Why does the seeder treat content and user state so differently, and how do deterministic ids and the two conflict strategies express that rule?

keyPoints.text: Content in the database is only a cache of the source files.
keyPoints.quote: The database copy is a cache and can be regenerated at any time.

keyPoints.text: User state has no other copy anywhere.
keyPoints.quote: Its source of truth *is* the database. It exists nowhere else.

keyPoints.text: The governing rule is to refresh content but protect progress.
keyPoints.quote: refresh content freely, and never harm user state.

keyPoints.text: Ids come from authored slugs, so a re-seed hits the same rows.
keyPoints.quote: Ids are derived from authored slugs, not generated

keyPoints.text: The cost is that an authored id can never be renamed safely.
keyPoints.quote: an authored id is now a permanent public key.

keyPoints.text: Upserting content makes re-running the seed harmless.
keyPoints.quote: Run it once or fifty times and the content tables end up identical.

keyPoints.text: User rows are only created when missing, never overwritten.
keyPoints.quote: A re-seed must never reset someone's level to 1.

questions.prompt: Walk through how pruning removed content evolved from a hard delete to a soft delete, and what every reader of the data must now do.

keyPoints.text: Without pruning, deleted content would keep being scheduled.
keyPoints.quote: still scheduled and still shown to learners

keyPoints.text: The original prune cascaded through foreign keys into history.
keyPoints.quote: Pruning an item silently deleted every attempt and card for it.

keyPoints.text: An accidental rename therefore became invisible data loss.
keyPoints.quote: For an accidental rename, it is data loss that nobody sees.

keyPoints.text: The seeder now unpublishes rather than deletes.
keyPoints.quote: The seeder now unpublishes instead of deleting.

keyPoints.text: A soft delete only works if all queries honour the flag.
keyPoints.quote: Every reader has to respect the flag, or a soft delete is just a bug.

keyPoints.text: json_each passes the whole id list as a single parameter.
keyPoints.quote: takes the whole list as one JSON array

keyPoints.text: A dry run and a rename map are still missing.
keyPoints.quote: What is still missing: a **dry run**, and a **rename map**

questions.prompt: Explain the additive migration approach in migrate(): why CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is not enough, what properties the migration keeps, and what a grown-up version would add.

keyPoints.text: IF NOT EXISTS skips existing tables, so old databases never get new columns.
keyPoints.quote: **does nothing if the table already exists**

keyPoints.text: Resetting the database to get the column would destroy progress.
keyPoints.quote: would wipe their progress

keyPoints.text: Adding a defaulted column is backward compatible.
keyPoints.quote: Adding a nullable or defaulted column is backward compatible.

keyPoints.text: The migration inspects current state before acting, so it is safe to repeat.
keyPoints.quote: so running it twice is harmless

keyPoints.text: The generalised version diffs against an in-memory copy of the current schema.
keyPoints.quote: builds the **current** schema (`SCHEMA_DDL`) in an in-memory SQLite database

keyPoints.text: Columns that cannot be added in place make the seeder refuse loudly.
keyPoints.quote: any new column must be addable in place, or the seeder refuses loudly.

keyPoints.text: Without a ledger, a backfill cannot detect whether it already ran.
keyPoints.quote: There is no `schema_migrations` table recording what has run.

keyPoints.text: Renames need expand, migrate readers and writers, then contract.
keyPoints.quote: Non-additive changes need expand/contract.
